content: The 69th session of the World Health Assembly (WHA) emphasized the importance of delivering the Integrated Care for Older People (ICOPE) recommendations in a structured and integrated manner. This process involves five critical steps, as outlined in the guidelines. 1. Comprehensive Assessments and Care Plans: Effective interventions for older adults begin with a thorough assessment of their intrinsic capacity, which includes evaluating physical, mental, and social health. This assessment also considers associated conditions, impairments, behaviors, and risks that may impact future capacity, as well as the individual’s environment. Beyond traditional history-taking and physical examinations, the process must include an in-depth understanding of the person’s values, priorities, and preferences regarding their health and its management. Comprehensive assessments aim to identify underlying conditions such as hypertension, diabetes, and dementia, and establish pathways for appropriate referral and treatment. These assessments are essential for developing tailored care plans that are both acceptable and appropriate for the individual. They also unify different healthcare providers around the shared goal of maintaining intrinsic capacity and functional ability, ensuring necessary follow-ups and linking healthcare with social care. 2. Shared Decision-Making and Goal-Setting: Integrated care can only be achieved if all services and providers work towards the common goal of preserving intrinsic capacity and functional ability. It is crucial to involve the older person in decision-making and goal-setting from the outset. Goals should align with the individual’s needs and preferences, ensuring that care is person-centered and respectful of their autonomy. 3. Strong Referral, Monitoring, and Support Systems: Regular and sustained follow-up of older individuals is vital for implementing the recommended interventions. This approach facilitates early detection of complications or changes in functional status, preventing unnecessary emergencies and inefficiencies. It also provides a platform for monitoring progress against the care plan and arranging additional support as needed. 4. Community Engagement and Caregiver Support: Caregiving for individuals with severely declining capacity can be demanding, often leading to caregiver isolation, psychological distress, and depression. Caregivers require basic information about the older person’s health conditions and practical skills, such as safe transfer techniques and assistance with bathing. They should also be informed about community-based resources and supported through strong referral pathways. Opportunities to involve communities and neighborhoods in caregiving should be explored, including encouraging local volunteering and enabling older community members to contribute. Associations and groups that bring older people together can serve as mechanisms for such activities. 5. Implementation and Adaptation: The ICOPE guidelines must be adapted into locally appropriate documents to meet the specific needs of each country and its health services. WHO headquarters will collaborate with regional and country offices, as well as implementing partners, to ensure effective communication and country-specific adaptation of these guidelines. This process includes analyzing budgetary and human resource requirements, identifying available inputs and systems, and determining areas needing additional investment. Training health workers, utilizing medical products and technologies, and adapting health information systems to collect data on intrinsic capacity and functional ability may require extra resources. An enabling environment should be created to support healthcare practitioners in using evidence-based practices, with local professional societies playing a key role in fostering an inclusive and participatory process. 6. Monitoring and Evaluation: The implementation of these recommendations will be monitored at community and health-facility levels. Data will be collected through surveys or updated service availability lists. Special studies may be conducted where routine monitoring is not feasible. A monitoring and evaluation framework, including core indicators, will be developed and included in the ICOPE country toolkit. These indicators will measure service delivery performance, feasibility, and acceptability of the recommendations. An international working group of experts will oversee these activities, ensuring that national adaptations of the guidelines result in legitimate, effective, equitable, and community-responsive programs. 7. Future Review and Updates: The WHO Department of Ageing and Life Course will regularly monitor new evidence in priority areas with the assistance of collaborating centers. Feedback from country implementation teams will be collected to refine ICOPE products. The guidelines will be updated every four years using a rigorous methodology, and suggestions for additional issues to include in future guidelines are welcomed. These ICOPE guidelines and associated products are essential tools for implementing the WHO Global Strategy and Action Plan on Ageing and Health. Dissemination efforts include publishing systematic reviews and evidence in peer-reviewed journals, as well as presentations and workshops at key conferences. By 2020, pilot testing and evaluation of these guidelines were planned in 20 countries, with monitoring and evaluation frameworks developed to measure their impact on health outcomes and service delivery.
